title: Gradio has a conflict with Python file cp1252
body:
### Describe the bug

When running gradio file.py, the code compiles. When opening the provided link for the gradio interface, the code crashes, giving the following error:

```
  File "C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python38\lib\encodings\cp1252.py", line 23, in decode
    return codecs.charmap_decode(input,self.errors,decoding_table)[0]
UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x8f in position 309911: character maps to <undefine>
```


After hours of trial and error, switching Python versions, using a new virtual environment, changing gradio version and more, I found a temporary solution: comment the code of file: cp1252.

This solves the issue for now.

Regarding the error I found that "0x8f" is part of the charmap of Python, but it's an undefined character, I cannot find more information on what is triggering this error.

def transcribe(inputs, task):

        )
    try:
        asr_client = Client(WHISPER_SERVER_PORT)
        result = asr_client.predict(inputs=inputs, task=task, api_name="/predict")

title: [Core] idle nodes fail to scale down due to idle_time_ms resetting
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Idle worker nodes (0 GPU/CPU usage, no scheduled tasks) never scale down while other nodes in the cluster are still running tasks. 
Also, activity shows up as "Busy workers on node" and "Resource: GPU currently in use" even when node is idle and idle counter is accumulating. 

Expected: each node's idle timer accumulates independently and triggers  scale-down after `idle_timeout_minutes` regardless of peer node activity

Actual: `idle_duration_ms` resets simultaneously on ALL nodes whenever a worker lease is released on ANY node, so the idle timer never accumulates past the inter-task interval

Hypothesis: the `WorkFootprint`/leased-worker tracking introduced to fix "blocked task" misclassification appears to reset `idle_duration_ms` cluster-wide as a side effect of worker lease lifecycle  events. The autoscaler.py scale-down decision is correctly per-node, but the `idle_duration_ms` signal from `GetClusterResourceState` is being corrupted by unrelated nodes' lease events

Related to #60546 , #60581 

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray version: 2.54.0
- OS: Linux (GCP)
- Python version: Python 3.10.12
- GPU: 4x nodes × 2x V100
- Autoscaler: v2

title: [core][experimental] ray.get of accelerated DAG result may not throw exception for MultiOutputNode
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

When calling `ray.get()` on the outputs of an accelerated DAG with a MultiOutputNode, we currently block on the results one at a time. This means that if one of the actor tasks threw an exception, we do not throw it until after we get the results for all of the previous actors' results, according to the order in the MultiOutputNode. This is a problem for tensor-parallel inference, because all of the workers execute in lockstep, and if one actor throws an exception, the others may hang. Depending on the order of the actors, `ray.get()` may never return.

We should fix this by trying to simultaneously get all of the outputs in the MultiOutputNode. One way is to try to `ReadAcquire` the channels in round-robin order.

### Versions / Dependencies

3.0dev

body: ### What happened + What you expected to happen We have a Ray cluster scheduled on EKS via the Kuberay operator. Our internal process submits remote jobs to these clusters on a regular basis. However, we've observed a consistent increase in memory and CPU usage of the Ray head. Notably, we're not running any Spark or heavy jobs on these clusters, just some basic Python scripts that occasionally involve pandas. We've tested this across all versions from Ray 2.5 to 2.32 and noticed similar behavior. Upon investigating the process consuming memory/CPU, we identified three key issues: 1. The Ray dashboard agent is consuming a significant portion of CPU and memory, with an excessive number of file descriptors open for log files. 2. Submitting more jobs in a shorter interval leads to a drastic increase in CPU and memory usage, which doesn't decrease even after the jobs are completed. In contrast, sparse job submissions have a less severe impact. 3. Once CPU usage reaches 30% - 40 %, we start experiencing job submission failures via Ray remote. title: [Bug] Possible tune / core bug related to correct resuming of trials on a dynamic cluster
body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues) and found no similar issues.


### Ray Component

Ray Core, Ray Tune

### What happened + What you expected to happen

I ve had a discussion on slack with @krfricke  about a recent tune bugfix that came with this PR (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/20536) which is among other things concerned with  correct resuming of trials... I myself always had problems in my setup with resume after a few days, so I installed the latest master nightly build  which included that PR and started running some tune session on my cluster. It went smoothly and I thought that bug has solved my problem, but then I got the following "Reset" on the night from 22nd to 23rd. 

Attached you find two pictures from the validation loss for a tune job with 70 tune trials (I run 7 discrete settings with tune.GridSearch() and num_samples=10, so 10 repeats per grid point and 70 total).
 ![training_run_step](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6616661/150848720-16831136-a35b-4ca5-9013-10c7abfc8049.png)
![training_run](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6616661/150848737-663c9d83-fa83-4a42-94db-ef81b86efd5f.png)

You can see that a bunch of trials get reset to the beginning and start over. In the second plot vs walltime it shows that trials stopped working on Jan 22nd .. they then stalled for a while and are only now being reset . 

I should say something about my somewhat peculiar cluster setup: I run on a SGE grid engine where I have 24 hour worker slots .. what I do currently is I have one ray master node that is permanently on a separate machine. On this machine I start ray via 
`subprocess.run(["ray",  "start" ,"--head" ,"--num-cpus=1" , "--num-gpus=0", "--temp-dir=%s" % ray_logdir], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)`
which works as the master node.

Additionally I run a cronjob which creates 3 new worker nodes as SGE slots every hour, and 3 workers crash every hour when their respective SGE slot ends.. so every hour 3 workers are basically crashing, and 3 new workers are added to ray.

On the worker nodes, I execute
`os.system("ray start --address='%s' --redis-password='5241590000000000' --num-cpus=1 --num-gpus=0 --temp-dir=%s" % (head_ip, ray_logdir))`
to connect to the master node.

Furthermore, on the master node, I then call a python script which first executes `ray.init()` to connect to the cluster and then `tune.rune( )` to run the tune trials.

Because I add 3 workers per hour, and each is 24 hour long, I get a total of 72 nodes permanently on, which can handle my 70 trials. So I have continuous crashing+resuming, which means I rely on correct resuming .. as you can see resuming worked perfectly until the hickup on jan 22/23 . Now, the remaining few trials are still at a standstill and so their progress basically stopped at jan 22/23rd wth the exception of the one trial that is running on the head node. The cluster status tells me 70/70 trials are running, which is definately not the case.. the majority is still stopped and the ones that are running have been reset to the beginning.
 Any idea what this could be or how I could debug this? I really want to solve this... in my opinion it should be possible to set up ray to be stable even if the cluster status is as dynamic as in my case.


**UPDATE**: I just killed the tune job on the head node, left ray running, and restarted the tune job with -resume .. it actually failed to restart with : 
`
Failed to get the system config for raylet because it is dead. Worker will terminate. Status: GrpcUnavailable: RPC Error message: failed to connect to all addresess; RPC Error details:`

I also found a few "too many open files" errors in raylet.err, could they have something to do with this? Does this relate to the log files that are created ? My log folder size from this 1 week of running is 30 GB with tons of files and I have used log_to_file=True. I am currently running again with the option "log_to_file=False", and see what happens. 
I have over 1900 log files in the logdir of the ray session, and over 900 files in the "old" subdirectory. The vast majority of the 30 GB comes from  hundreds of raylet files which are each 80 MB.

**UPDATE2**: 
After running a second time for a week, with "log_to_file=False" (but resume=True probably has overwritten this) the same errors appear and the system seems to be hanging again. Another error I just now discovered is in dashboard.log, of the type:


`2022-01-24 17:31:43,188 ERROR node_head.py:241 -- Error updating node stats of 6ae37dcaf2c024fba86ceb92c1d7b9dd6aed518a0b8c1cf17e956ce9.
Traceback (most recent call last):
    raise _create_rpc_error(self._cython_call._initial_metadata,
grpc.aio._call.AioRpcError: <AioRpcError of RPC that terminated with:
        status = StatusCode.UNAVAILABLE
        details = "failed to connect to all addresses"
        debug_error_string = "{"created":"@1643041903.188611088","description":"Failed to pick subchannel","file":"src/core/ext/filters/client_channel/client_channel.cc","file_line":3134,"referenced_errors":[{"created":"@1643041903.188609397","description":"failed to connect to all addresses","file":"src/core/lib/transport/error_utils.cc","file_line":163,"grpc_status":14}]}"`

Any ideas?

### Versions / Dependencies

2.0.0 nightly build (from ~17th of january 2022), python 3.89, scientific linux 7

### Reproduction script

Currently no script available.

### Anything else

This isse has occured multiple times, but I thought the latest bugfixes with the above mentioned pull release would have fixed it

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

title: [core] ScheduleAndGrantLeases: O(N×M) redundant GCS liveness checks per scheduling round
body:
## Summary

`ScheduleAndGrantLeases()` calls `NodeAvailable()` — a GCS liveness lookup — for every (pending lease, candidate node) pair. At 50 nodes and 2000 pending tasks, that's 100,000 redundant calls per scheduling round. Each call goes through mutex + `StringIdMap::Get` + `NodeID::NodeID` construction.

The Raylet event loop is single-threaded. `ScheduleAndGrantLeases()` runs synchronously — no heartbeat, network event, or GCS update can interleave. A node that was alive at the start of the round is still alive 2 seconds later when the round ends. Yet every (lease, node) pair asks the question again.

## Call chain

```
ScheduleAndGrantLeases()
  for each pending lease (N):
    GetBestSchedulableNode()
      scheduling_policy_->Schedule()
        for each candidate node (M):
          IsSchedulable()
            NodeAvailable() → GCS liveness lookup
```

## Fix

Snapshot node liveness once at round start, then consult the snapshot for O(1) hash set lookup.

`BeginSchedulingRound()` iterates all nodes via `NodeAvailableInternal()` (original logic) and populates a `flat_hash_set`. `NodeAvailable()` returns `snapshot.contains(node_id)` when a round is active. `EndSchedulingRound()` clears it.

6 files, 177 lines. RAII guard ensures begin/end pairing on all exit paths.

## Correctness

The single-threaded event loop makes the snapshot trivially correct — liveness is invariant during the round. The snapshot needs no invalidation, no locks. The depth counter handles nested scheduling rounds defensively.

## Evidence

- 42/42 existing tests pass, no regressions
- New test `SchedulingRoundSnapshotCallCount`: 500 ops across 50 nodes → 500 `IsNodeAlive` calls without snapshot, 50 with snapshot (GMock `.Times()` verified)
- New test `SchedulingRoundSnapshotSemantics`: verifies snapshot create/use/destroy lifecycle
- 8-node GH200 perf: `GetBestSchedulableNode` visible in head raylet profile during heavy scheduling
- 3 rounds of independent agent review; thread safety audited (all callers on main thread)

title: [Serve]Constructor failure tests don't account for replica id changing across restarts
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Several constructor failure tests in `test_gang_scheduling.py` and` test_constructor_failure.py` use replica_id.unique_id to identify replicas across constructor retries. However, when a replica fails during construction, Ray Serve stops the actor and creates a new one with a fresh unique_id. This means any logic that compares the current replica's id to a previously stored id will never match after a retry, making those code paths unreachable.

### Affected tests
1. #### `python/ray/serve/tests/test_gang_scheduling.py`
 - `test_startup_failure_stops_entire_gang`
The test stores the first failing replica's unique_id and later tries to block any replica matching that id so the test driver can observe an intermediate state :

```
failed_replica_id = ray.get(failed_replica_store.get.remote())
# ...
if replica_id == failed_replica_id:
    ray.get(recovery_signal.wait.remote())
```
Since the retried replica has a new unique_id, the condition never matches and `recovery_signal.wait()` is never called. The test still passes because the controller's reconciliation loop introduces enough natural delay for the intermediate assertion, but this is timing dependent rather than deterministic.

- `test_partial_constructor_failure`
The docstring says it "validates gang deployment where one replica consistently fails," but the implementation uses the same pattern:

```
if replica_id == failed_id:
    raise RuntimeError(...)
```
On retry the new replica has a different unique_id, so this branch never executes. The test behaves identically to the adjacent `test_transient_constructor_failure `, one failure followed by full recovery to HEALTHY with all 4 replicas RUNNING. The "consistent failure" scenario described in the docstring is untested.

2. #### `python/ray/serve/tests/test_constructor_failure.py`
- `test_deploy_with_partial_constructor_failure ` Uses replica_id to re match the failed replica on retry:
```
failed_id = ray.get(store.get.remote())
if replica_id == failed_id:
    raise RuntimeError("Consistently throwing on same replica.")
```
This branch never fires. The test passes because the retry gets a new replica_id, succeeds, and the deployment goes HEALTHY with 2 replicas, identical to the transient test below it.

I have a working fix locally for gang_scheduling failures, that replaces replica_id based store with a gang_id keyed helper actor that deterministically decides which gang should fail and which should block.
- Rewrites `test_partial_constructor_failure` to cover the distinct "one gang permanently fails, deployment stuck in UPDATING" scenario.
- Fixes `test_startup_failure_stops_entire_gang` to deterministically block retry gang replicas using gang_id instead of relying on controller timing.
-  The fix for normal replica failure tests is slightly different
Happy to submit a PR if this looks good.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray: 3.0.0.dev0
Python: 3.11.13
OS: macOS 

### Reproduction script

To confirm the blocking logic:
pytest -xvs python/ray/serve/tests/test_gang_scheduling.py::TestGangFailureRecovery::test_startup_failure_stops_entire_gang
Comment out the` recovery_signal.send()` call in the test body. If the blocking branch were actually working, removing the signal that unblocks it should cause the test to hang forever. Instead, the test still passes at the same speed .

title: [Core] GCS kv store has no cleanup or eviction strategy for pickled function during job lifetime
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

When a Ray job registers remote functions or actor classes via function_manager.export(), the pickled function/actor metadata is stored in GCS internal KV under the fun namespace (`KV_NAMESPACE_FUNCTION_TABLE`). These entries are never cleaned up while the job is still running, and the KV store has no eviction strategy to reclaim space from stale entries.

The only cleanup mechanism exists in `GCSFunctionManager`, which uses reference counting per job. Cleanup is triggered solely when `RemoveJobReference(job_id)` decrements the counter to zero — which happens only when the job finishes and all detached actors from that job are dead.

Ray's documentation explicitly states that [redefining remote functions in a loop](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/ray-core/patterns/redefine-task-actor-loop.html) is an anti-pattern, as each ray.remote() call registers a new function entry in GCS that never gets cleaned up.

However, [FunctionNode._execute_impl()](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/1927658ad6a97788bd86fc59310d1ed45a08e60e/python/ray/dag/function_node.py#L44) calls ray.remote(self._body) on every execution:

```python
def _execute_impl(self, *args, **kwargs):
    return (
        ray.remote(self._body)
        .options(**self._bound_options)
        .remote(*self._bound_args, **self._bound_kwargs)
    )
```

This means every DAG execution triggers a new ray.remote() registration, creating a new KV entry in GCS — exactly the anti-pattern the documentation warns against. Applications built on Ray DAG that execute repeatedly will accumulate unbounded function metadata in GCS KV.


### Versions / Dependencies

ray=2.53

### Reproduction script

> The real compute logic is more complex so we use `ray.dag` instead of `ray.data`.

```python
import ray
import time
import random
from typing import List

# Add pickled_function_size to about 4M, so we can reproduce it faster. We don't really use data transfer like this.
global_tensor = torch.randn(1000, 1000)

@ray.remote
def inference_model_node(input_text: str) -> str:
    local_tensor = global_tensor + 1
    time.sleep(random.uniform(1, 2))
    return f"Inferred({input_text})"

@ray.remote
def aggregate_model_node(base_input: str, *inference_results: str) -> str:
    time.sleep(random.uniform(10, 10))
    num_deps = len(inference_results)
    return f"Aggregated ({base_input})_from_[{num_deps}_deps]"

if ray.is_initialized():
    ray.shutdown()
ray.init()

NUM_AGGREGATE_NODES = 200
NUM_MODEL_PER_AGGREGATE = 100

all_aggregate_nodes = []

from memory_profiler import profile

@profile
def main():
    # aggregate node
    aggregate_results = []
    for i in range(NUM_AGGREGATE_NODES):
        if len(aggregate_results) > 20:
            ready_refs, aggregate_results = ray.wait(aggregate_results)
            results = ray.get(ready_refs)
            print(f'Finished results: {results}')

        inference_dependencies = []
        # model node
        for j in range(NUM_INFERENCE_PER_AGGREGATE):

        aggregate_results.append(aggregate_node.execute())

    results = ray.get(aggregate_results)
    print(f'Last batch results: {results}')

    start_time = time.time()

    end_time = time.time()
    print(f"\Results: {final_result}")
    print(f"Time: {end_time - start_time:.2f} 秒")

title: [Serve][Core] RayService upgrade can return HTTP 500 when ray start receives SIGTERM before Serve proxy drains
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Related KubeRay issue: https://github.com/ray-project/kuberay/issues/4799

`TestRayServiceZeroDowntimeUpgrade` in KubeRay can fail during old RayCluster termination after a RayService upgrade. The test continuously sends traffic to the RayService Serve endpoint and expects all requests to succeed:

```python
assert num_failures == 0, f"num_failures: {num_failures}"
```

The observed failure is a burst of HTTP 500 responses from old Serve proxies:

```text
POST,/,LocustBadStatusCode(code=500),20
```

Packet captures showed that these are real HTTP responses from Uvicorn, not just TCP resets:

```http
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
server: uvicorn
connection: close

Internal Server Error
```

The issue appears to be triggered by a container process-tree change between the Ray 2.32 and Ray 2.33 images.

In the older image, Bash remains PID 1:

```text
PID 1:  /bin/bash -c 'ulimit -n 65536; ray start --block ...'
PID 13: ray start --block ...
```

When Kubernetes deletes the pod, it sends `SIGTERM` to PID 1. In this process tree, Bash receives the signal first and Ray does not immediately start its own shutdown. The old Serve proxy and old Serve replicas tend to remain alive together until the pod is eventually killed, which hides the shutdown-ordering bug.

In the newer image, the resulting process tree has `ray start` as PID 1:

```text
PID 1: ray start --block ...
```

Now Kubernetes sends pod-termination `SIGTERM` directly to `ray start`. That exposes the bad shutdown ordering:

```text
Kubernetes deletes old pod
-> SIGTERM is delivered to ray start
-> Ray starts tearing down local processes
-> Serve replicas can become unavailable
-> old Serve proxy is still alive on existing keep-alive connections
-> old proxy receives a request but has no usable replica
-> old proxy returns HTTP 500
```

Expected behavior:

When `ray start --block` receives `SIGTERM`, Ray should give Serve proxies on that node a bounded chance to drain network traffic before local replicas and Ray processes are torn down.

At a high level, the desired shutdown order is:

```text
SIGTERM to ray start
-> mark local node draining in GCS
-> Serve observes the draining node
-> Serve proxy stops accepting/reusing HTTP/gRPC traffic
-> active requests/RPCs finish or hit the drain deadline
-> ray start continues local process teardown
```

A draft solution with this flow has been implemented and it passed the same test. Happy to contribute a PR if the diagnosis sounds right.

### Versions / Dependencies

Observed around the Ray image migration:

```text
Passing image behavior: rayproject/ray:2.32.0-py310
Failing image behavior: rayproject/ray:2.33.0-py310
```

Controlled comparisons from the KubeRay investigation:

```text
Ray 2.32 code in Ray 2.33 image environment: failed
Ray 2.33 code in Ray 2.32 image environment: passed
Matched Python/package Ubuntu 20.04 image: passed
Matched Python/package Ubuntu 22.04 image: failed
```

Relevant environment:

```text
Kubernetes: v1.29.0
Runtime:    containerd 1.7.1
Kernel:     Linux 6.8.0-90-generic
Test:       ray-operator/test/e2erayservice/rayservice_ha_test.go
            TestRayServiceZeroDowntimeUpgrade
```

### Reproduction script

The reproduction is currently the KubeRay e2e test from: https://github.com/ray-project/kuberay/issues/4799

High-level reproduction flow:

1. Create a RayService and wait for it to become ready.
2. Create a separate RayCluster that runs Locust.
3. Send HTTP traffic to the RayService Serve endpoint using persistent connections.
4. Update the RayService to trigger zero-downtime cluster replacement.
5. Delete/terminate the old RayCluster as part of the upgrade flow.
6. Observe that existing keep-alive connections pinned to old Serve proxies can receive HTTP 500 responses.

Direct confirmation of the PID 1 mechanism:

The Ubuntu 22.04 container command was changed from effectively:

```bash
ulimit -n 65536; ray start --block ...
```

to:

```bash
ulimit -n 65536; ray start --block ...; wait
```

The trailing command prevents Bash from replacing itself with `ray start`, restoring Bash as PID 1. With this change, the Ubuntu 22.04-based image passed repeated runs with no relevant failures. This confirms the immediate trigger.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

title: [Data] Get correct logical resource usage
body:
### Description

`TaskPoolMapOperator` and `ActorPoolMapOperator` report logical resource usage based on statically-defined `ray_remote_args`

https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/1f45462bd8339e838d50aece2b8547216b6f135e/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/task_pool_map_operator.py#L140-L146

However, if `ray_remote_args_fn` is defined, then the operator can launch tasks with more logical resources than the statically defined `ray_remote_args`. This leads to resource manager undercounting logical resource usage.

https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/1f45462bd8339e838d50aece2b8547216b6f135e/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/map_operator.py#L504-L516

### Proposal solution

We should record the actual resources used whenever we launch a task, so that when we call `current_logical_usage`, we can get the actual logical resource usage.

https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/1f45462bd8339e838d50aece2b8547216b6f135e/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/task_pool_map_operator.py#L110-L111

```python
def _try_schedule_task(...):
  ...
  dynamic_ray_remote_args = self._get_dynamic_ray_remote_args(input_bundle=bundle)
  self._curr_resources["cpu"] += dynamic_ray_remote_args["cpu"]
  ...
  # callback function to remove resources after task done

def current_logical_usage(self) -> ExecutionResources:

title: [Core] Permanently stuck objects/tasks
body:
## Summary

When many workers on a single node recycle simultaneously due to `max_calls`, their input objects can be evicted from the plasma store. The pull manager on other nodes retries forever against the stale location because the object owner is never notified of the eviction. This causes Ray Data streaming tasks to hang permanently with no failure raised.

## Root Cause

Three mechanisms chain together to produce a permanent hang:

### 1. `max_calls` thundering herd causes mass pin release

Workers that started around the same time all hit the `max_calls` limit together. In the observed incident, 73 workers on a single node disconnected simultaneously (`graceful=true, disconnect_type=1`). Each disconnect releases the worker's pin references on objects in the local plasma store via `DisconnectClient()` in `node_manager.cc`.

### 2. Plasma evicts the unpinned objects

With high memory pressure (e.g. `MapBatches` configured with `memory=12884901888`), the suddenly-unpinned objects are immediately eligible for LRU eviction. Objects that are inputs to pending tasks on *other* nodes get evicted before those tasks can pull them.

### 3. Pull manager retries forever against a stale location

The pull manager asks the `OwnershipBasedObjectDirectory` for the object location. The owner (driver) reports the original node — it was **never notified of the eviction**. The pull manager sends pull requests to that node, gets plasma errors (object not found), and retries with exponential backoff.

Critically, `pull_manager.cc` only arms a failure expiration timer when the object has **no locations**. Since the owner reports a (stale) location, the timer is never set. The pull manager retries indefinitely.

### Why reconstruction doesn't trigger

The driver already handed the `ObjectRef`s to downstream task arguments and doesn't call `ray.get()` on them. There is a known gap in `node_manager.cc`'s `DisconnectClient()`:

```cpp
// TODO(rkn): Tell the object manager that this client has disconnected so
// that it can clean up the wait requests for this client. Currently I think
// these can be leaked.
```

Nobody tells the owner the objects are gone → the owner never triggers reconstruction → the pull manager retries a stale location forever.

## Observable Behavior

- **Ray Data**: reports `num_tasks_running: N` tasks that never make progress, with `num_tasks_failed: 0`
- **Ray Core**: scheduler shows `num_tasks_waiting_for_workers: 0` and empty infeasible queue — tasks appear placed but are silently blocked on object resolution
- **Dashboard**: tasks are invisible in the running-task list but futures are still pending
- **Raylet state dump**: `num chunks received failed / plasma error` and `PullManager: num pull retries` counts frozen at high values
- **Training**: continues consuming already-produced blocks, then deadlocks when the split queue is exhausted

The net effect is a silent hang — no error is raised, no timeout fires, and no metric transitions to a failure state.

## Reproduction

1. Set up a Ray Data streaming pipeline with a `max_calls`-limited operator (e.g. `MapBatches` with `max_calls=50`)
2. Use enough workers on a single node that many hit the call limit simultaneously
3. Ensure high object store memory pressure so eviction is immediate
4. Observe upstream operator tasks stuck in RUNNING state with `pending_task_inputs > 0`

The thundering herd is more likely with:
- Large `num_cpus` per task (fewer workers per node → more synchronized call counts)
- Uniform task durations (workers progress through calls at the same rate)
- High task throughput (workers hit `max_calls` in a short window)

## Observed Incident

- **Job**: 10-node cluster (r5d.metal, 96 CPU / 565 GB object store each)
- **Pipeline**: `Input → StreamingRepartition[num_rows_per_block=1] → MapBatches(_fused_transforms) → split(8, equal=True)`
- **Trigger**: 73 workers recycled simultaneously on one node at 10:37:00
- **Result**: 8 StreamingRepartition tasks stuck for >2h24m (67,887/68,029 blocks produced, 142 missing), 6,328 plasma errors, 25,106 pull retries, zero tasks failed
- **Impact**: Training progressed to 71% on already-produced blocks before deadlocking

### Key log evidence

**ray-data.log** (1,711 consecutive identical 5-second snapshots):
```
StreamingRepartition - Tasks: 8; Blocks Outputted: 67887/68029
```

**Operator metrics** (frozen):
```
num_tasks_running: 8
num_tasks_finished: 3832
num_tasks_failed: 0
obj_store_mem_pending_task_inputs: 8216908
```

**raylet.out** (node 10.231.67.72):
```
num chunks received failed / plasma error: 6328
PullManager: num pull retries: 25106
num_tasks_waiting_for_workers: 0
Infeasible queue length: 0
```

## Suggested Fixes

1. **Notify object manager on worker disconnect** — resolve the TODO in `DisconnectClient()` so evicted objects trigger owner notification and reconstruction
2. **Stale location detection in pull manager** — after N consecutive pull failures from the same location, query the owner for a fresh location or arm the expiration timer
3. **Stagger `max_calls` recycling** — add jitter to the `max_calls` limit (e.g. `max_calls ± random(0, max_calls * 0.1)`) to avoid thundering herd disconnects
4. **Ray Data-level timeout** — detect operators with stuck `num_tasks_running > 0` and `num_tasks_failed == 0` for an extended period and raise an error or cancel/resubmit the stuck tasks

title: [autoscaler] Autoscaler replacement failure after `ALLOCATION_TIMEOUT` in KubeRay clusters
body:
## Summary
In KubeRay-based Ray clusters, when a worker instance enters `ALLOCATION_TIMEOUT`, the autoscaler may fail to terminate the timed-out instance before issuing a replacement launch request.

As a result, the timed-out instance can continue to consume `replicas/maxReplicas` capacity, preventing the replacement worker from being created and breaking automatic recovery.

## Problem Description
When a Ray Autoscaler v2 managed KubeRay worker times out during allocation, the system should automatically terminate that instance and launch a new worker to restore the desired cluster capacity.

However, the current implementation in `Reconciler._step_next()` executes the side effects in this order:

1. `_handle_stuck_instances()`
2. `_scale_cluster()`
3. `_handle_instances_launch()`
4. `_terminate_instances()`

This means the launch request is submitted before the termination request in the same reconcile cycle. If the worker group is already at or near `maxReplicas`, the launch path still observes the timed-out worker in the current replica count, so the replacement worker may not be created.

In repeated reconcile cycles, this can show up as:

- replacement workers not starting successfully
- repeated retries involving `QUEUED` and `REQUESTED`
- eventual transition to `ALLOCATION_FAILED` after exhausting retries
- cluster capacity not recovering to the desired level

## Reproduction Steps
1. Create or use a KubeRay cluster with a worker group that has a configured `maxReplicas`.
2. Ensure the current worker count is already at or near that limit.
3. Cause one worker to remain stuck after allocation so that its instance eventually transitions to `ALLOCATION_TIMEOUT`.
4. Keep unsatisfied resource demand in the cluster so the autoscaler still needs to launch a replacement worker.
5. Observe the autoscaler reconcile behavior and the resulting RayCluster patches.

### Expected Behavior
- The `ALLOCATION_TIMEOUT` instance should be marked for termination first.
- The termination patch should be submitted before the replacement launch request.
- The replacement worker should be able to enter the normal launch flow.
- Cluster capacity should recover without being blocked by the stale timed-out instance.

### Actual Behavior
- The autoscaler attempts to launch a new worker before submitting termination.
- The launch path still evaluates capacity using the old replica view.
- The replacement worker may be blocked by `maxReplicas`.
- The timed-out worker is not replaced in time, leaving the cluster under-provisioned.

## Root Cause Analysis
The issue is caused by incorrect ordering of termination and launch side effects inside `Reconciler._step_next()`.

`_handle_stuck_instances()` first converts stuck instances into `ALLOCATION_TIMEOUT`, and `_scale_cluster()` can correctly decide that one more worker should be launched. But in the old flow, `_handle_instances_launch()` runs before `_terminate_instances()`.

For `KubeRayProvider`:

- launch logic derives the desired worker count from the current RayCluster worker group state
- that calculation still includes the timed-out worker because termination has not been submitted yet
- when the worker group is already constrained by `maxReplicas`, the replacement launch is capped or effectively becomes a no-op

So the scheduler is not missing the need for a replacement. The real problem is that the replacement launch is issued before capacity is released by the termination request.
label: actionable

title: [core] Default GCS thread number considers cgroup
body:
### Description

Hi team, currently we use multiple polling threads for GCS grpc client and server, the number of which is controlled here: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/9a6f32921ed5cafbb755b47ba12dce1a24eaa837/src/ray/common/ray_config_def.h#L407-L417

One issue that I found is: the default thread number is controlled by `std::thread::hardware_concurrency`, which doesn't consider cgroup effect. In production, kuberay RayJob is scheduled to beefy machine with hundreds of and thousands of logical cores, which leads to >10GiB ray head memory consumption even for a simple "helloworld" dumb task.

We could override the values by environment variables, of course, but I'm wondering if it's better for default values consider cgroup? Thank you!

Related issue in DuckDB: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/6519, which ends up with considering cgroup on linux.
I personally think the same patch is applicable to ray core as well.
Reference for DuckDB's cgroup thread number handling: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/30b7c8ca2c707a4a172dd5e41a2831059c7ec5de/src/common/cgroups.cpp#L182-L237

### Use case

N/A, issue description should be straightforward.

title: [Serve] HAProxy stats_port hardcoded to 8404 — no env var override
body:
### Ray version
`ray==2.55.1`

### Problem
Every port-like field on `HAProxyConfig` (`ray/serve/_private/haproxy.py`) reads from a `RAY_SERVE_HAPROXY_*` constant that honors an env var — except `stats_port`, which is hardcoded:

https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.55.1/python/ray/serve/_private/haproxy.py#L337-L348

```python
class HAProxyConfig:
    socket_path: str = RAY_SERVE_HAPROXY_SOCKET_PATH
    ...
    stats_port: int   = 8404                              # ← hardcoded
    metrics_port: int = RAY_SERVE_HAPROXY_METRICS_PORT    # env-overridable
```

The template unconditionally `bind *:{{ config.stats_port }}` ([haproxy_templates.py#L136](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.55.1/python/ray/serve/_private/haproxy_templates.py#L136)), so two HAProxy-mode Ray Serve proxies on the same host can't coexist (e.g. two `ray start --head` clusters used for benchmarking/CI).

### Suggested fix
Add `RAY_SERVE_HAPROXY_STATS_PORT` to `_private/constants.py` mirroring `RAY_SERVE_HAPROXY_METRICS_PORT`, and reference it in the dataclass default.
label: actionable

title: [Serve] No hard gate prevents new replicas/deployments during shutdown; race can leak actors
body:
### Problem

After the controller begins shutdown, the deployment manager **does not** consistently block creation of new replicas or new deployments. A TODO on `DeploymentStateManager.shutdown()` notes that **logic is still needed to prevent new replicas once the shutdown signal is sent**. In parallel, the same method’s docstring claims shutdown **does** prevent new deployments/replicas, which is **misleading** given the current code.

### Expected behavior

Once Serve shutdown has started (`DeploymentStateManager._shutting_down` / controller `_shutting_down`), **no new deployments**, **no upscale**, and **no new replica scheduling** should occur. API calls that would mutate goal state should fail fast or no-op with a clear error.

### Likely root cause

- `DeploymentStateManager.deploy()` does not check `_shutting_down` before creating deployments and applying target state.  
- Upscale paths (`scale_deployment_replicas`, `_add_upscale_replicas`, etc.) do not check DSM shutdown.  
- Controller deploy/config paths may still accept work while shutting down.

### Risk

Concurrent deploy or scaling work can create **STARTING** replicas (or scheduling requests) that are **not torn down** with the rest of Serve, producing **orphaned replica actors** and leaked resources.
label: actionable

title: [<RLlib>] Creating parallel envs with certain cpu allocation
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

## Ray Symmetric-Run CPU Affinity for Env Workers (HPC / Slurm)

I am running a **Ray symmetric-run** setup on an HPC cluster using **Slurm**. The cluster consists of:

* 32 nodes
* 128 CPU cores per node

For my custom RL Gym environment, I configure:

* `64` `env_runners`
* `60` CPUs per `env_runner`
* `48` environments per `env_runner`
* `2` `env_runners` per node (→ 96 environments per node)
* `gym.envs.registration.VectorizeMode.ASYNC` enabled

---

## The Problem

Each `env.step()` call launches an **external application**.

When too many environments execute in parallel, the external application slows down drastically due to resource contention. The slowdown becomes significant when many environments compete for CPU resources simultaneously.

---

## What Works Outside of Ray

When I run the same workload without Ray using `ProcessPoolExecutor`, I can mitigate the issue by explicitly setting CPU affinity per environment:

```python
os.sched_setaffinity(pid, {cpu_number})
```

By pinning worker processes to specific CPU cores, I can prevent excessive CPU contention. This approach works reliably.

---

## What I Want to Achieve in Ray

I would like to replicate this CPU pinning behavior within Ray symmetric-run. Specifically:

* Assign specific CPU cores to each environment worker's env. So like if I have 2 workers with 4 envs, first worker should use cpu0 for first env, cpu1 for the second env, etc...
* Prevent multiple environments from competing for the same CPU cores
* Control CPU affinity similarly to how it is done with `ProcessPoolExecutor`

---

## Question

Is there a way to force Ray `env_runners` to use specific CPU cores for their environments via:

* `PPOConfig`, or
* Ray resource configuration, or
* any other Ray mechanism?

Any guidance on best practices for CPU affinity control in Ray (especially in HPC/Slurm environments) would be greatly appreciated.


### Versions / Dependencies

ray = 2.54.0
python = 3.15
os = linux

### Reproduction script

Sadly it is not possible to reproduce since I cannot share the external application.

### Issue Severity

High: It blocks me from completing my task.

title: [Serve][LLM] FastAPI >= 0.137 breaks metrics middleware: '_IncludedRouter' object has no attribute 'path'
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Ray Serve's LLM metrics middleware crashes with `AttributeError: '_IncludedRouter' object has no attribute 'path'` and returns **HTTP 500 on every matched request**, when the served FastAPI app uses `include_router(...)` and FastAPI >= 0.137 is installed.

**Root cause:** FastAPI 0.137 ([fastapi/fastapi#15785](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/15785)) changed `app.routes` so routes added via `include_router()` are wrapped in `_IncludedRouter` objects that have **no `.path` attribute**. In `python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/observability/metrics/middleware.py`, `_get_route_details()` iterates `app.routes` and reads `starlette_route.path` unconditionally on FULL/PARTIAL matches, so it raises `AttributeError`.

```
File ".../ray/llm/_internal/serve/observability/metrics/middleware.py", line 134, in _get_route_details
    route = starlette_route.path
AttributeError: '_IncludedRouter' object has no attribute 'path'
```

This is the same root cause that affected OpenTelemetry (open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python-contrib#4699), Elastic APM, and prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator.

**Expected:** the middleware resolves the templated route (e.g. `/api/items/{item_id}`) for the metric tag without crashing, on FastAPI >= 0.137.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: master (latest)
- FastAPI: 0.137.2 (Ray pins `fastapi>=0.133.0` with no upper bound, so 0.137+ installs by default)
- Python: 3.11
- OS: Linux

### Reproduction script

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from ray.llm._internal.serve.observability.metrics.middleware import (
    _get_route_details,
)

app = FastAPI()
router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/items/{item_id}")
def get_item(item_id: str):
    return item_id


app.include_router(router, prefix="/api")  # FastAPI 0.137 wraps this in _IncludedRouter

scope = {
    "type": "http",
    "method": "GET",
    "path": "/api/items/123",
    "headers": [],
    "app": app,
    "path_params": {},
    "root_path": "",
}

# Raises: AttributeError: '_IncludedRouter' object has no attribute 'path'
print(_get_route_details(scope))
```

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

title: [Data] Move streaming output backpressure escape hatch to apply across all backpressure policies
body:
**Description**

The `_should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure` escape hatch currently lives inside `ReservationOpResourceAllocator` and only takes effect when the *resource budget* policy returns 0 bytes to read. When a *different* backpressure policy (e.g., `DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy`) independently returns 0, the escape hatch is never consulted and the operator can deadlock. The fix is to move the escape hatch to a layer where it applies regardless of which policy triggered the backpressure.

**Background**

Ray Data's streaming executor applies backpressure through a list of `BackpressurePolicy` objects. During each scheduling loop iteration, [`process_completed_tasks`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/0c2c5f56d4/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/streaming_executor_state.py#L451-L476) iterates over all policies, calls `max_task_output_bytes_to_read(op)` on each, and takes the **minimum** (most restrictive) value. If the final result is 0, the operator cannot read any outputs from its running tasks.

There are currently two policies that can return 0:

1. **`ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy`** — delegates to [`ReservationOpResourceAllocator.max_task_output_bytes_to_read`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/0c2c5f56d4/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/resource_manager.py#L937-L957). When `res == 0`, it calls `_should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure` and bumps the result to 1 if the escape hatch fires.

2. **`DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy`** — [`max_task_output_bytes_to_read`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/0c2c5f56d4/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py#L224-L229) returns a hard `0` when `_should_apply_backpressure` is true. It has **no** escape hatch.

The escape hatch ([`_should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/0c2c5f56d4/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/resource_manager.py#L721-L770)) exists to prevent deadlocks / livelock. It checks whether downstream operators are starved (no active tasks, no queued inputs, resource-constrained, or idle for too long) and, if so, allows at least 1 byte to be read. This is a correctness/liveness mechanism, not a performance optimization — it must apply universally.

**Motivation**

When the `DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy` triggers output backpressure, an operator's running tasks can produce data but the executor cannot read it. If the downstream operator is simultaneously starved for input (e.g., it has no active tasks and no queued blocks), the pipeline stalls: upstream can't release outputs, downstream can't get inputs. The escape hatch was designed to prevent exactly this scenario, but because it's buried inside the resource allocator, it doesn't fire when a different policy is the bottleneck.

**Implementation Boundaries & Constraints**

- The escape hatch logic currently lives in `OpResourceAllocator._should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure` (resource_manager.py:721). It needs to move to a place that runs **after** all policies have been consulted and the final `max_bytes_to_read` has been computed.
- A place to implement this could be in `process_completed_tasks` (streaming_executor_state.py:451-476), where the per-policy minimums are already aggregated. When the aggregated result is 0, the escape hatch could bump it to 1. But think hard about what the cleanest implementation would look like. It could be elsewhere.
- The escape hatch depends on topology state and the resource manager (downstream eligible ops, `can_submit_new_task`, `has_external_consumer`, `num_waiting_consumers`, idle detection). Make sure these dependencies remain accessible at the new call site.
- Preserve the existing behavior for the resource budget policy path — the change should be additive, not a regression for pipelines that only use that policy.
label: actionable

title: [Data] BlockMetadata.input_files causes excessive object store memory usage when passing datasets to Ray Train workers
body:
## What happened + What you expected to happen

When passing Ray Datasets (created from **millions of parquet files**) to `TorchTrainer`, we observe **~12.87 GB of pinned objects per worker** in the Ray object store. This causes excessive disk spillage and memory pressure.

**Expected**: Dataset handles should be lightweight references that don't bloat when serialized to workers.

**Actual**: `BlockMetadata.input_files` stores all source file paths, and these are serialized with the dataset when passed to training workers.

## Root Cause Analysis

### The Data Flow

```
read_parquet(paths)  # millions of S3 paths
    → FileBasedDatasource.get_read_tasks()
        → DefaultFileMetadataProvider._get_block_metadata()
            → BlockMetadata(input_files=paths)  # ALL paths stored here
    → DatasetStats(metadata={"Read": [read_task.metadata, ...]})
        → ExecutionPlan(stats)  # stored as _in_stats
            → Dataset._plan._in_stats.metadata  # BLOATED
```

### The Problematic Change

**Commit**: `384f46cbb80` (June 12, 2024)
**PR**: #45860 - "Remove `in_blocks` parameter of `ExecutionPlan`"

This commit (part of the LazyBlockList removal effort) changed how `DatasetStats` is created:

**Before**:
```python
block_list = LazyBlockList(read_tasks, ...)
return Dataset(plan=ExecutionPlan(block_list, block_list.stats(), ...))
```

**After**:
```python
stats = DatasetStats(
    metadata={"Read": [read_task.metadata for read_task in read_tasks]},
    parent=None,
)
return Dataset(plan=ExecutionPlan(stats, ...))
```

The full `BlockMetadata` objects (including `input_files` with millions of file paths) are now directly stored in `DatasetStats.metadata`.

### Where input_files is populated

**File**: `python/ray/data/datasource/file_meta_provider.py:156-161`

```python
def _get_block_metadata(self, paths: List[str], ...) -> BlockMetadata:
    return BlockMetadata(
        num_rows=num_rows,
        size_bytes=...,
        input_files=paths,  # <-- All source file paths
        exec_stats=None,
    )
```

### Impact

When using Ray Data + Ray Train with large parquet datasets:
- `BlockMetadata.input_files` contains **millions** of S3/file paths
- The bloated metadata is stored in `dataset._plan._in_stats.metadata`

**The critical issue: Dataset is serialized N times for N workers**

When `TorchTrainer` initializes workers, it serializes the Dataset object and passes it as an argument to each `RayTrainWorker.init_train_context()` call:

```
TorchTrainer.fit()
    → For each of N workers:
        → RayTrainWorker.init_train_context.remote(train_run_context, dataset_shard_provider)
            → train_run_context contains: datasets dict (serialized)
            → dataset_shard_provider contains: DataIterator with base dataset (serialized again)
```

This means:
- **N workers × 2 copies per worker** (TrainRunContext + DatasetShardProvider) = **2N serialized copies**
- Each copy includes the full `_in_stats.metadata` with millions of file paths
- With 8 workers: 16 copies of the bloated metadata pinned in object store
- Result: **~12.87 GB of pinned objects per worker** observed via `ray memory`

The serialization overhead scales linearly with both:
1. Number of input files (millions of paths in `input_files`)
2. Number of training workers (each receives full serialized dataset)

## Proposed Solutions

### Option 1: Don't populate `input_files` at all (Ray Data scope)

**Pros**:
- Simplest fix
- Benefits all Ray Data use cases
- `input_files` appears to be only for debugging/stats, not execution

**Cons**:
- Breaking change for users who rely on `dataset.input_files()` API
- Loss of provenance tracking

**Implementation**:
```python
# file_meta_provider.py
return BlockMetadata(
    num_rows=num_rows,
    size_bytes=...,
    input_files=None,  # or []
    exec_stats=None,
)
```

### Option 2: Clear metadata when dataset is passed to Ray Train (Ray Train scope)

**Pros**:
- No impact on Ray Data standalone usage
- Preserves `input_files` for debugging in non-Train scenarios

**Cons**:
- Train-specific workaround, doesn't help other serialization scenarios
- Requires Train to know about Data internals

**Implementation** (what we did as a workaround):
```python
# In TorchTrainer or DataConfig
def _clear_dataset_stats_metadata(datasets):
    for key, dataset in datasets.items():
        plan = getattr(dataset, '_plan', None)
        if plan:
            in_stats = getattr(plan, '_in_stats', None)
            if in_stats and hasattr(in_stats, 'metadata'):
                in_stats.metadata = {}
```

### Option 3: Store input_files as object reference (Ray Data scope)

Similar to how `FileBasedDatasource` stores paths, use `ray.put()` to store the input_files list in the object store and keep only a reference in `BlockMetadata`.

**Pros**:
- Preserves full `input_files` information
- Only one copy in object store, referenced by all workers
- Consistent with existing patterns in Ray Data

**Cons**:
- More complex implementation
- Requires careful lifecycle management of the object reference
- May need schema changes to `BlockMetadata`

**Implementation sketch**:
```python
# When creating BlockMetadata
input_files_ref = ray.put(paths) if len(paths) > threshold else None

return BlockMetadata(
    num_rows=num_rows,
    size_bytes=...,
    input_files=[] if input_files_ref else paths,
    input_files_ref=input_files_ref,  # New field
    exec_stats=None,
)
```

## Recommendation

**Option 1** (don't populate `input_files`) is the cleanest solution if the field is not critical for execution. The `input_files()` API could be deprecated or made to return an empty list with a warning.

If backward compatibility is required, **Option 3** (object reference) provides a good balance between preserving information and avoiding serialization bloat.


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray version: 2.52.1
- Python version: 3.12
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04

### Reproduction script

```python
import ray
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer
from ray.train import ScalingConfig

ray.init()

# Read from millions of parquet files (e.g., a large production dataset)
# The issue manifests when input_files contains millions of S3 paths
ds = ray.data.read_parquet("s3://bucket/path/with/millions/of/files/")

def train_fn(config):
    pass

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_fn,
    datasets={"train": ds},
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=8),
)

# Check object store before fit()
# ray memory --stats-only

trainer.fit()
```

Run `ray memory` to observe large pinned objects from `RayTrainWorker.init_train_context`.

### Issue Severity

None

title: [Autoscaler] Cluster-level idle termination for Ray Autoscaler V2
body:
### Description

Related: https://github.com/ray-project/kuberay/issues/4768

## 1. Motivation

The Ray Autoscaler today scales **worker** pods to zero based on per-node-type `idleTimeoutSeconds`, but the **head pod, head Service, and the RayCluster CR itself** persist even when no Ray jobs, actors, or placement groups are active. For users who back the head with reserved capacity, the leftover cost is non-trivial.

This RFC proposes a new `autoscalerOptions.idleTerminationSeconds` field. When set, the autoscaler observes whether the entire cluster has been idle past the threshold and reports an `IdleTerminationExpired` status condition on the RayCluster CR. The KubeRay operator observes the condition and decides the terminal action. The autoscaler stays in an observer role; the operator remains the sole owner of cluster lifecycle.

The design is scoped to **Autoscaler V2** and the **KubeRay provider** only. V1 and non-KubeRay providers are out of scope.

## 2. Proposed Solution
### 2.1 New `autoscalerOptions.idleTerminationSeconds` field
```yaml
spec:
enableInTreeAutoscaling: true
autoscalerOptions:
idleTimeoutSeconds: 60 # existing: per-worker scale-down
idleTerminationSeconds: 1800 # NEW: cluster-wide idle threshold
```
`idleTerminationSeconds` is **V2-only and KubeRay-only**. Default unset = feature disabled; existing CRs see no behavior change.
The two fields are orthogonal: `idleTimeoutSeconds` scales worker pods to zero (cheap, reversible); `idleTerminationSeconds` triggers full cluster termination (expensive, owner-decided).

### 2.2 Annotation emitted by autoscaler

When the predicate fires, the autoscaler patches a single annotation on the RayCluster CR. The KubeRay operator observes the annotation and performs the terminal action.

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    ray.io/idle-ttl-expired: "true"
```

Operator behavior (KubeRay-side, sketch):

```go
if rc.Annotations["ray.io/idle-ttl-expired"] == "true" {
    r.recorder.Eventf(rc, corev1.EventTypeNormal,
        "IdleTTLExpired", "Cluster idle past idleTerminationSeconds; deleting")
    return ctrl.Result{}, r.Delete(ctx, rc)
}
```

The annotation is one-shot: once set, the operator reconciles and deletes the CR; the autoscaler sidecar dies along with the head pod. 


### Use case

_No response_

title: [Serve]App-level policy state loss and shared dict corruption (followup to #58857)
body:
There are 2 issues in the way app-level autoscaling state is handled inside `_apply_app_level_autoscaling_config`:
1. State dropped for skipped deployments : When an app-level policy omits a deployment from its decisions, the wrapper discards any user state the policy returns for that deployment, returning only raw internal state. User accumulated state is lost on the next control loop.
2. Shared state dict corrupts internal state across deployments : If the policy returns the same dict object as state for multiple deployments, `_merge_user_state_with_internal_state` mutates it in-place . The first deployment's internal keys leak into the shared dict, corrupting delay logic for subsequent deployments.

title: Support .tar.gz archives for remote working_dir URIs
body:
## Feature Request

### What is the problem this feature solves?

When using `working_dir` in `runtime_env` with a remote S3 URI pointing to a `.tar.gz` archive, Ray raises:

```
ValueError: Only .zip files supported for remote URIs.
```

This is enforced in `python/ray/_private/runtime_env/working_dir.py`:

```python
if protocol in Protocol.remote_protocols() and not path.endswith(".zip"):
    raise ValueError("Only .zip files supported for remote URIs.")
```

Many CI/build systems (Bazel, pip, conda, etc.) produce `.tar.gz` archives as their primary artifact format. Requiring `.zip` forces users to add a conversion step (download tar.gz → repackage as zip → re-upload), which adds latency, storage overhead, and complexity — especially in KubeRay/RayJob workflows where the submitter pod must perform this conversion at runtime.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Extend `working_dir` remote URI support to accept `.tar.gz` (and `.tgz`) archives in addition to `.zip`.

Ray's `download_and_unpack_package` in `packaging.py` already uses `smart_open` for downloading and Python's standard library has built-in `tarfile` support, so the implementation should be straightforward:

1. Update the validation in `working_dir.py` to allow `.tar.gz` / `.tgz` extensions
2. Update `download_and_unpack_package` to detect the archive format and use `tarfile.open(..., "r:gz")` for tar archives
3. Update documentation to reflect the new supported formats

### Alternatives considered

- **Repackage tar.gz to zip at runtime**: Works but adds latency (download + repack + re-upload) and doubles storage for every job submission
- **Custom init container**: Mount a Kubernetes init container to download and extract the tar.gz before Ray starts — bypasses Ray's runtime env entirely and loses benefits like automatic working directory setup and PYTHONPATH management
- **Build system changes**: Modify CI to produce zip instead of tar.gz — not always feasible when the build system (e.g. Bazel `py_binary` / `pkg_tar`) natively produces tar.gz

### Additional context

This is particularly relevant for KubeRay / RayJob CRs where `runtimeEnvYAML` specifies `working_dir` pointing to a CI-built archive in S3. The current `.zip`-only restriction creates friction for organizations whose build pipelines produce `.tar.gz` artifacts.

title: [dashboard] k8s_utils.cpu_percent() crashes with ZeroDivisionError on nodes registered with num-cpus=0
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

## Description

`k8s_utils.cpu_percent()` raises `ZeroDivisionError` on every metrics poll cycle for any Ray node
registered with `--num-cpus=0`. The exception is caught and returns `0.0`, so behavior is functionally
correct, but `logger.exception()` logs a full traceback on every call, spamming pod logs.

## Reproduction

Deploy a KubeRay cluster with `num-cpus: "0"` on the head node (the documented best practice):

```yaml
# raycluster.yaml — from Ray's own docs recommendation
headGroupSpec:
  rayStartParams:
    num-cpus: "0"   # Recommended to prevent tasks scheduling on head
```

Any pod with `num-cpus: "0"` will produce repeated errors in the dashboard agent logs:

```
ERROR ray.dashboard.k8s_utils - Error computing CPU usage of Ray Kubernetes pod.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../ray/dashboard/k8s_utils.py", line 49, in cpu_percent
    cpu_percent = round(quotient * 100 / get_num_cpus(), 1)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```

## Root cause

In `python/ray/dashboard/k8s_utils.py`:

```python
cpu_percent = round(quotient * 100 / get_num_cpus(), 1)  # ← ZeroDivisionError when get_num_cpus() == 0
```

Interestingly, the same developer already guarded against this exact scenario elsewhere in
`reporter_agent.py` (same file that calls `k8s_utils`):

```python
# _get_load_avg() in reporter_agent.py — correctly guarded ✅
if self._cpu_counts[0] > 0:
    per_cpu_load = tuple(...)
else:
    per_cpu_load = None
```

The guard was simply missed in `k8s_utils.cpu_percent()`.

## Impact

Affects **every KubeRay deployment** that follows the documented `num-cpus: "0"` recommendation
(head nodes, zero-CPU specialized worker groups). The Ray docs explicitly recommend this pattern:
> *"setting num-cpus:'0' for the Ray head pod will prevent Ray workloads from being scheduled on the head"*

## Fix

One-line change in `python/ray/dashboard/k8s_utils.py`:

```python
# Before
cpu_percent = round(quotient * 100 / get_num_cpus(), 1)

# After
cpu_percent = round(quotient * 100 / (get_num_cpus() or 1), 1)
```

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray 2.44.0

### Reproduction script


No K8s cluster needed — the bug can be triggered locally by simulating the two conditions:
`get_num_cpus()` returning 0 (as it does on `--num-cpus=0` nodes) and cgroup CPU stats being
readable (mocked here).

```python
"""
Minimal reproduction of k8s_utils.cpu_percent() ZeroDivisionError.
Simulates a Ray node started with --num-cpus=0 inside a K8s pod.

Run with:  pip install ray && python repro.py
"""
import time
from unittest.mock import patch

import ray.dashboard.k8s_utils as k8s_utils

# Simulate two successive cgroup reads so cpu_delta > 0 (triggers the division)
cpu_reads = iter([1_000_000_000, 2_000_000_000])
sys_reads  = iter([10_000_000_000, 20_000_000_000])

with (
    patch.object(k8s_utils, "_cpu_usage",    side_effect=cpu_reads),
    patch.object(k8s_utils, "_system_usage", side_effect=sys_reads),
    patch.object(k8s_utils, "_host_num_cpus", return_value=8),
):
    # Prime last_* so the second call computes a real delta
    k8s_utils.cpu_percent()

    # Simulate --num-cpus=0: get_num_cpus() returns 0
    from ray._private import utils as ray_utils
    with patch.object(ray_utils, "get_num_cpus", return_value=0):
        result = k8s_utils.cpu_percent()
        print(f"Result: {result}")  # returns 0.0 (exception caught)
        # Check logs — should show ZeroDivisionError traceback
```

Expected output (stderr):
```
ERROR ray.dashboard.k8s_utils - Error computing CPU usage of Ray Kubernetes pod.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../k8s_utils.py", line 49, in cpu_percent
    cpu_percent = round(quotient * 100 / get_num_cpus(), 1)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```


### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

title: [Bug] test_streaming_split_invalid_iterator is flaky with wrong error type from _barrier()
body:
The test expects a `ValueError` when too many concurrent consumers use the same split.
Instead, a bare `assert` in `_barrier()` fires first and raises `AssertionError`, which the test does not catch.

### Root cause

Two different invalid-consumer conditions are detected in _barrier() and get(),
but they raise inconsistent error types:
```
_barrier() L369-372  ->  bare assert  ->  AssertionError   (racing through the barrier, causes flakiness)
get()      L255-258  ->  raise ValueError                  (consumer calling with a stale epoch id)
```

Both in [`stream_split_iterator.py`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/data/_internal/iterator/stream_split_iterator.py)
The assert in _barrier() should be a ValueError to match get() and satisfy pytest.raises(ValueError) in the test.


### Fix

Replace the bare `assert`s in `SplitCoordinator._barrier()` ([lines 369-372](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/data/_internal/iterator/stream_split_iterator.py#L369-L372)) with `ValueError`:

```python
# Before
assert self._output_iterator is not None
assert self._cur_epoch == starting_epoch + 1, f"Expected ... (got {self._cur_epoch})"

# After
if self._output_iterator is None:
    raise ValueError("Invalid iterator: output iterator is not initialized.")
if self._cur_epoch != starting_epoch + 1:
    raise ValueError(
        f"Invalid iterator: too many concurrent consumers detected. "
        f"Expected epoch {starting_epoch + 1}, got {self._cur_epoch}."
    )
```

### References
- Related PR: #61190
- Flaky CI run: https://buildkite.com/ray-project/postmerge/builds/16626#019d1e72-8628-4f29-9963-24a3a911bac3

---

title: BUG: bdate_range returns one less days when end and periods are given
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
assert len(pd.bdate_range(end='20260320', periods=3)) == 3
assert len(pd.bdate_range(end='20260321', periods=3)) == 3  # fail

### Issue Description

As of pandas 3.0.0, `bdate_range` returns one fewer element than expected when `end` falls on a weekend.

However, `pd.bdate_range(end="20260321", periods=3)` returns:

I would expect this call to still return 3 business dates, ending at the last business day before the weekend.

title: PERF: High overhead in stack frame warning inspections (find_stack_level)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Whenever pandas raises a warning, it invokes `find_stack_level()` to trace the call stack and identify the calling context outside of pandas. Currently, this function walks the stack frames and calls `inspect.getfile(frame)` inside a loop:

```python
while frame:
    filename = inspect.getfile(frame)
    if filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir):
        frame = frame.f_back
        n += 1
```

For workloads that emit multiple warnings (or libraries relying heavily on pandas warnings), this function is highly inefficient because:
1. `inspect.getfile(frame)` is slow as it does lookup caching, module parsing, and absolute path validation inside the interpreter loop.
2. It repeatedly imports `pandas` and resolves `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths on *every* warning invocation.

### Proposed Optimization
1. Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level.
2. Retrieve the filename directly via `frame.f_code.co_filename` instead of calling `inspect.getfile(frame)`.

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked 500,000 runs of the original stack inspection vs. the optimized caching and `co_filename` check on a local environment:

| Implementation | 500,000 runs | Overhead per call |
|---|---|---|
| **Original (`master`)** | 3.67 seconds | ~7.33 microseconds |
| **Optimized** | 0.19 seconds | ~0.38 microseconds |

This yields a **~19x speedup** (95% reduction in call overhead).

title: BUG: pd.to_datetime segfaults on Series of duplicated ISO8601 strings (regression in 3.0.4)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/pandas/) of pandas (3.0.4).
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas. (Reproduced on the latest released 3.0.4; happy to retest on main if a wheel/build is provided.)

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# 50 unique ISO8601 timestamp strings, repeated up to 3000 rows
base = [f"2000-01-01T0{i % 9}:00:00.000" for i in range(50)]
vals = [base[i % len(base)] for i in range(3000)]

pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(vals))   # Segmentation fault (core dumped) on 3.0.4
print("SUCCESS - no segfault")
```

Run with `python -X faulthandler repro.py`.

### Issue Description

`pd.to_datetime()` on a `Series` of duplicated ISO8601 timestamp strings **segfaults** (process dies with `Segmentation fault (core dumped)`, exit code 139) on **pandas 3.0.4**. There is no Python exception; the interpreter crashes in native code.

The crash requires:
- A sufficiently large series (reproduces at ~3000 rows; does **not** reproduce at ~2000), and
- Many duplicate values (the input factorizes to a small number of unique timestamps, which routes through the `map_array` / `take` fast path).

`faulthandler` backtrace (identical for both the synthetic reproducer above and our real-world data):

```
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00007ffffef6d780 (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/core/dtypes/missing.py", line 194 in _isna
  File ".../pandas/core/dtypes/missing.py", line 174 in isna
  File ".../pandas/core/dtypes/missing.py", line 672 in is_valid_na_for_dtype
  File ".../pandas/core/arrays/datetimelike.py", line 614 in _validate_scalar
  File ".../pandas/core/arrays/_mixins.py", line 170 in take
  File ".../pandas/core/arrays/datetimelike.py", line 2584 in take
  File ".../pandas/core/array_algos/take.py", line 108 in take_nd
  File ".../pandas/core/algorithms.py", line 1705 in map_array
  File ".../pandas/core/arrays/base.py", line 2745 in map
  File ".../pandas/core/base.py", line 1020 in _map_values
  File ".../pandas/core/series.py", line 4675 in map
  File ".../pandas/core/tools/datetimes.py", line 1038 in to_datetime
  File "repro.py", line 8 in <module>
```

### Version bisection

Tested in `python:3.13-slim` (linux/amd64), wheels only, identical reproducer and data:

| pandas | numpy  | result   |
|--------|--------|----------|
| 2.3.3  | 2.4.6  | OK       |
| 3.0.0  | 2.4.6  | OK       |
| 3.0.1  | 2.4.6  | OK       |
| 3.0.2  | 2.4.6  | OK       |
| 3.0.3  | 2.4.6  | OK       |
| **3.0.4** | **2.4.6** | **SEGFAULT** |
| **3.0.4** | **2.3.4** | **SEGFAULT** |

The regression was introduced in **pandas 3.0.4** (3.0.3 is fine) and is **independent of the numpy version**. Deterministic: reproduces on every run.

### Expected Behavior

`pd.to_datetime()` should return a datetime Series (or raise a normal Python exception), never segfault the interpreter.

### Installed Versions

- python: 3.13.14 (official `python:3.13-slim` image, GCC 14.2.0), linux/amd64
- pandas: 3.0.4
- numpy: 2.4.6 (also reproduced with 2.3.4)
- Install: `pip install --only-binary=:all:` (manylinux wheels)

Originally surfaced via a downstream project where `pd.to_datetime` on a column of ~361k timestamp strings (many duplicates) crashed CI on Python 3.13. Minimized to the 6-line synthetic reproducer above.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from time import perf_counter


def bench(nrows: int, indexer_kind: str, selection_fraction: float, repeat: int = 3) -> float:
    n_set = max(1, int(nrows * selection_fraction))
    take_idx = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(nrows, size=n_set, replace=False)

    if indexer_kind == "bool":
        indexer = np.zeros(nrows, dtype=bool)
        indexer[take_idx] = True
    else:
        indexer = take_idx

    value = np.datetime64("2020-01-01", "ns")
    times_ms = []
    for _ in range(repeat):
        ser = pd.Series(np.empty(nrows, dtype=object))
        t0 = perf_counter()
        ser.iloc[indexer] = value
        times_ms.append((perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)

    return min(times_ms)


for case in [
    (1_000_000, "bool", 0.01),
    (1_000_000, "bool", 0.5),
    (10_000_000, "bool", 0.01),
    (10_000_000, "ndarray", 0.01),
]:
    print(case, f"{bench(*case):.1f} ms")

title: Suggestion: link a RAG / LLM debugging checklist (WFGY Problem Map) in the docs
body:
Hi pandas team,

thank you for maintaining such a foundational library. pandas is often the first stop for people who are building data workflows that later feed into LLM or RAG systems (corpus cleaning, chunking, metadata enrichment, offline evaluation, and so on).

I maintain an MIT-licensed project called **WFGY Problem Map**, which is a 16-question diagnostic checklist for RAG / LLM pipelines in production. It focuses on data and retrieval failure modes (ingestion gaps, chunking pathologies, vector store issues, evaluation leaks, etc), not on model weights.

Why I think this might be relevant for pandas users:
- Many real-world RAG systems start from pandas DataFrames (documents, logs, event streams) before anything is embedded or indexed.
- Several of the 16 failure modes are about how tabular and semi-structured data are transformed and filtered before they reach a retriever.
- The checklist is tooling-agnostic and can be applied no matter whether people use pandas alone or in combination with other frameworks.

For credibility: the same checklist has already been included in a few curated / academic ecosystems such as
- ToolUniverse by Harvard MIMS Lab  
- Multimodal RAG Survey by QCRI LLM Lab  
- Rankify (University of Innsbruck)

Suggestion:

If you think it could be useful for your users, would you consider adding a small link in your docs or resource section such as

> “RAG / LLM debugging checklist: WFGY Problem Map (16 failure modes)”  
> https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY/blob/main/ProblemMap/README.md

Project home: https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY

Thanks again for all your work on pandas and for considering this small suggestion.

Best,  
PSBigBig

title: ENH/BUG: Utilize `_values_for_json` in `Series.to_json`
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

ExtensionArrays can define a `_values_for_json` method if the standard numpy array with `object` dtype returned by `__array__` is not serializable because the objects themselves are not serializable. However this method is only utilized for `DataFrame.to_json` trough `BlockManager.column_arrays`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/core/internals/managers.py#L1249-L1251

In `Series.to_json` no path leads to the `_values_for_json` method and nearly always `__array__` is utilized. Therefore some ExtensionArrays are only JSON serializable if they are in a `DataFrame` and not a `Series`, which in my opinion also could be considered a bug.

### Feature Description

In short modify the `objToJSON.c` file to also call `_values_for_json` for pandas `Series`.

With the help of GitHub Copilot I was able to trace the issue to the `get_values` function, specifically the following lines:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L201-L213

- In `201` we are effectively calling `Series.values` and assign it to `values`.
- If the `Series` and therefore `values` is not empty `values` now is a numpy array or ExtensionArray.
- Next in `205` it is checked if `values` has a `__array__` attribute and if so calls it, that is also the path mentioned above that leads potentially to the numpy array of object dtype with not serializable objects in it.
- At last in `210` if none of the checks above worked it is checked if `values` is already a `np.ndarray` (and only that, so no subclass) and if not dereferences `values` and tries to create the array somewhere up the stack (if I understand it correctly).

My proposal would be to add another check after the empty check but before the `__array__` check. Similar to the `__array__` check it could test if `values` has a `_values_for_json` attribute (and therefore is an ExtensionArray) and if so calls that method to create the serializable numpy array. This check could work like the following snippet, but I have not tried it out yet. It would be important to include it before the `__array__` check as ExtensionArrays have that attribute too:
```c
else if (PyObject_HasAttrString(values, "_values_for_json")) {
    // We have gotten an ExtensionArray
    PyObject *array_values = PyObject_CallMethod(values, "_values_for_json", NULL);
    Py_DECREF(values);
    values = array_values;
}
```
Disclaimer: This snipped was developed with GitHub Copilot after chatting with it to understand how the `get_values` function works and asking if a check similar to `__array__` would also work in the designated spot. It also suggested to not make it an `else if` block but an `if` block so that if the return value of `_values_for_json` itself is not already a `np.ndarray` but an array-like object the following checks could still convert that object using the `__array__` attribute. In my opinion that is not necessary because the function signature of `_values_for_json` already specifies that the return value shall be a `np.ndarray` and the base implementation just calls `np.asarray(self)` which should also dispatch to `__array__`. I therefore modified the snipped above accordingly. As there currently do not seem to be any test for `_values_for_json`, adding tests that make sure that this method actually returns an `np.ndarray` and that the values inside are serializable seems sensible.

### Alternative Solutions

Always convert your `Series` to `DataFrame` with `sr.to_frame()` before JSON serialization, then the `_values_for_json` method of the ExtensionArray is already used.

### Additional Context

I found this issue during my work for an external ExtensionArray to support astropy `Quantity` objects which are subclasses of `np.ndarray` but themselves not JSON serializable.

I also looked a bit around through the open issues regarding `Series` and JSON serialization and found #55426 by @jbrockmendel, there he wrote down some general notes about formatting of ExtensionArrays, the proposed enhancement is especially connected to point 6 of the list.

title: PERF: pandas.io.sql.has_table slow for ADBC driver with large database
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

We actually noticed the slowness from `pandas.read_sql`, but narrowed the problem down to its call to `has_table`. We're calling `read_sql` with a query so it will always be a miss for `has_table`.

```python
import time
import pandas.io.sql as pd_sql
from adbc_driver_snowflake.dbapi import connect

with connect("<database URI>") as conn:  # Connection to a large database
    start = time.perf_counter()
    pd_sql.has_table("foo", conn)  # Where foo does not match a table
    end = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"Took {end - start} seconds")
```

The problem sees to be in [`pandas.io.sql.ADBCDatabase.has_table`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/sql.py#L2429-L2431), which calls [`self.con.adbc_get_objects()`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.Connection.adbc_get_objects) without passing `depth=`. The default depth is `"all"`, which enumerates objects down to the columns. Adding `depth="tables"` speeds things up dramatically for us—from 53 seconds without `depth="tables"` down to 3 seconds with.
